scenes.narration: Can an attractive image tell us how it was calculated? We will distinguish the roles through DLSS5, examine actual exposure and focus demonstrations, then inspect a frame's inputs and outputs. Displayed frames and game calculations have different responsibilities; we begin with what reconstruction is asked to do.

DLSS 4 Multi Frame Generation was introduced in 2025 with support for adding up to three generated frames per rendered frame under supported conditions. Its output is display frames; it does not imply three additional sets of ray samples.

In 2026, DLSS 4.5 expanded Super Resolution and Multi Frame Generation features. Its 6X mode must be understood as up to five generated frames per rendered frame. Dynamic operation considers display targets and execution conditions; it does not promise 6X operation on every device.

Keep one actually rendered frame as a white block. Adding three generated frames gives four displayed blocks; adding five gives six. More generated blocks do not mean that the game has performed its simulation that many times.

In the recorded comparison, inspect both the moving image and its interface. A larger displayed frame-rate number does not establish more frequent responses to input. After this short demonstration, separate rendered and generated blocks again to distinguish display updates from game updates.

DLSS 5 was announced in 2026 and became available in NBA 2K27 in September. NVIDIA describes using game color, motion, and 3D guidance to improve the appearance of lighting and materials. We discuss the vendor's input-output description without claiming our own quality measurements of that game.

Creators can use controls such as strength, color treatment, and exclusions to preserve artistic intent. These controls connect the feature's output to the intended design. They should be distinguished from exact computation of every physical light path.

Compare the same responsibility across different games. The first three sources are March2026 DLSS5 previews. Read Off and On first, then examine the light on faces and clothing. The September basketball release is a separate example.

Start with Resident Evil, moving from a dark room to the rainy vehicle shot. Watch the turning face and wet clothing. The labelled On condition changes their surface appearance. Different poses are not a pixel-aligned ground truth.

Starfield provides an orange coat and suits in brighter interiors. The dialogue UI identifies a character; it is not a quality score. Lighting differs from the rainy scene, but the question remains: where does the final appearance of light on skin and fabric change?

Hogwarts Legacy moves through an interior, a street and an underground shot. At each cut, select the new face and clothing. Compare Off and On within that shot. A glowing wand or visible steam alone does not establish new physical simulation.

Now examine skin, jerseys and arm highlights on the basketball court. The close Detroit number-two shot changes from Off to On; subsequent dunks use other camera angles. This compares displayed appearance, not ball physics or input response. Compare those surfaces with dark wet clothing, a bright coat and underground fabric: the same display-stage task meets different surface conditions.

After comparing surfaces in four games, establish an observation reference in this2022 Hogwarts showcase. The character in yellow climbs stairs below bright windows. Identify the clothing, windows and shaded wall.

Outside, the same clothing is framed by sky and stone pillars. The camera looks up at the towers, then follows the stairs. The character remains the reference, while background and viewing direction change. Record those conditions when comparing images.

At the balustrade, nearby stone and distant landscape share one image. Red identifies the nearby rail; another color identifies the distant view. Looking down changes occlusion too. This is why brightness comparisons need the observation position as well.

The camera turns around the character near a burning brazier. Follow the flame, clothing and stone floor separately. A bright flame and a lit surface are different observation targets; one region alone does not describe the entire image.

Back in the hall, the character appears dark against a bright window. Turning the camera moves the window and carved decorations within the image. Identify the window, clothing and stairs in that order. A consistent reference makes color and exposure changes easier to read.

Finally, approach a character beneath the tree. The Talk prompt identifies an interaction target; our red mark identifies the clothing under observation. Keep the game's instructions distinct from our comparison marks.

Throughout this progression, actual computation, temporal reconstruction, and display-frame generation should remain distinct. Comparisons record hardware support, game version, internal resolution, and latency. A higher version number does not mean every preceding function has merged into one replacement.

We compared surface appearance across four games. Next, control a cause directly: exposure and focus can change the image without moving lights. Connect editor settings to results, then inspect the actual resources inside a frame.
Lighting results are not yet the colors sent directly to a monitor. Bright values can exceed a display's range. Exposure and tone mapping connect that wider range to the final display range.

Separate the lighting value from the displayed value. An illustrative linear intensity of two with an exposure multiplier of one-half feeds a value of one into tone mapping. The light itself has not changed. Tone mapping applies a separate curve, so the final display is not explained by that multiplication alone.

Exposure scales scene brightness, while tone mapping applies nonlinear transformations such as highlight compression. Automatic exposure can change the whole image without a lighting change, so technical comparisons need controlled exposure conditions.

This is a2017 Unreal editor demonstration. Separate the cube arrangement from the post-process controls on the right. Camera and parameters both change, so we first identify the edited inputs rather than attributing every brightness difference to one feature.

This editor demonstration adjusts exposure settings rather than rearranging the lights. Follow the controls alongside the image brightness. It illustrates how the displayed result can change even when the lighting setup remains the same. That is why we must match exposure before comparing reconstruction features.

The exposure panel shows lower and upper brightness limits and a bias. Reading those settings differs from measuring displayed pixel intensity. Keep the same bright and dark cube faces in view while following the changes.

The demonstration switches to histogram visualization. It adds information for reading a brightness distribution instead of showing only the ordinary image. Connect the lower graph to the controls. Its green and blue colors are visualization, not the wall material colors.

The visualization explicitly names a logarithmic scale. Equal horizontal spacing does not mean an equal additive brightness change. It displays a wide dark-to-bright range in one view. Read the scale before relating graph position to brightness.

Camera movement changes the proportions of surfaces in the image. Seeing more bright cubes can change the brightness distribution within the same lit scene. Exposure comparisons therefore need camera framing as well as settings. This is an observation demonstration, not a fixed-camera numerical experiment.

We can now separate three roles: edited settings, diagnostic visualization and the final image. Settings are inputs; the graph helps inspection; the displayed image includes later display processing. A diagnostic graph color is not itself a final surface pixel color.

Bloom adds the appearance of bright regions spreading into neighboring pixels. A glowing image does not establish that indirect illumination reached surrounding surfaces. Bloom around an edge is not proof of a light bounce.

In the bloom controls, distinguish spread around bright regions from the cube surfaces themselves. A wider glow and light bouncing onto another surface answer different questions. Inspect the edited effect rather than treating a bright impression as proof of an indirect-lighting implementation.

Next come color and tone controls. The cubes remain while their displayed appearance can be adjusted. Earlier chapters created scene lighting; this stage maps its result into a display range. Distinguish computing the input from shaping its presentation.

Use both a bright face and a shaded face on the same cube. Looking only at highlights can miss contrast changes; looking only at shadows can miss highlight compression. Follow the control and both regions to distinguish overall changes from changes concentrated in a brightness range.

A darker-looking surface does not by itself establish that its material asset changed. Here we observe post-process controls and their results. A claim about material inputs requires inspecting those inputs separately. Similar image changes can originate at different stages.

Read brightness and color balance as separate aspects of grading. Keep the cube arrangement as a reference and identify the chosen control. A warmer or cooler appearance can resemble a changed light color without establishing the same underlying operation.

Keeping the same surface preserves a reference for comparison. Red follows the observed face; another color identifies the setting. The mark is an observation location, not a game-world distance or physical unit. Reacquire the surface when the camera changes.

Record the edited input, the surface where a change appears and any simultaneous condition changes. Next we examine a separate color-transform resource, continuing the distinction between final displayed color and the original lighting value.

First locate the setting that will apply the color transform. The demonstrator selects the area labelled Post Process Blendable and searches for blend in the right panel. The scene cubes and the effect settings have separate roles. Establish where the next resource will be connected.

The panel shows a post-process material entry, followed by a lookup-table asset displayed as a strip of colors, or LUT. It represents color correspondence rather than a small map of the game world. After identifying the color resource, distinguish distance and focus in the same cube arrangement.

Depth of field represents differences in focus and distance, while motion blur approximates movement over an exposure interval. These effects can conceal small shadow or reflection errors or introduce their own blur. Comparisons should distinguish enabled and disabled conditions.

Before reading focus regions, inspect what becomes blurred in the ordinary view. Use the cube arrangement to distinguish near and far edges. The Scale control changes the amount of blur. This is a historical2017 Bokeh demonstration; its value is not a physical camera f-stop.

Visible blur alone does not identify the responsible distance region. The visualization menu therefore leads to a focus-region display. Once diagnostic colors and their legend appear, distinguish them from material colors. We can then inspect the focus reference and the boundaries around it.

Read the focus legend first: blue marks far regions, green near regions and black the focused region. These are not cube material colors. As distance and transition settings are edited, distinguish the focus reference from the width of its transition.

Focus distance and transition width are not the same quantity. One establishes a reference location; the other relates to the surrounding change range. Read the edited field before inspecting the affected regions, without pairing different settings as an identical-condition On/Off comparison.

Next, inspect focus. Separate near, focused and far regions in the debug view, then return to the scene and observe blur on the nearer object. Here the blur is connected to focus controls. Recording those conditions prevents us from confusing it with a reconstruction error in a reflection.

Back in the ordinary view, a nearer cube appears blurred. Separate diagnostic colors from ordinary scene colors. Camera and focus-related settings also change in this demonstration, so record those conditions when explaining the blur.

When focus effects are enabled during reconstruction comparisons, a blurred edge can be misattributed. Check focus and camera conditions first, then the reconstruction conditions. Separating stages lets similar-looking blur be explained by different causes.

The later editor interval retains the cube arrangement as a reference. Follow the selected control and compare near and far surfaces. An overall impression of blur can hide which distance region changed. Separating the focus reference and its surrounding regions makes the observation more specific.

Read the input name, locate its change, then inspect the affected surface. Record camera changes separately. This observation method transfers to other engines without assuming their internal post-process order is identical.

Check again whether color inputs represent linear values or display values. This closes the linear-space discussion from episode two. Missing or duplicated transformations at texture input, lighting, and final output produce incorrect brightness.
Final pixels combine geometry, visibility, lighting, materials, reconstruction, and post-processing. We can now examine how to trace those connections during frame inspection.

We compared final appearance in four games with editor exposure, color and focus controls. We can observe changes, but identifying which command read which resource is another question. Frame inspection now follows actual inputs and outputs rather than relying on feature names.

Before frame inspection, briefly follow the code that submits drawing commands. Distinguish the debugger’s yellow current-line mark from the caller list below it. The source connects closing a command list with requesting execution. A CPU paused on this line does not establish GPU completion.

Feature names alone do not determine a frame's actual structure. Engine version, platform, rendering path, and settings can change its passes. A frame debugger such as RenderDoc helps inspect commands and resources from a captured frame.

This is our channel’s simple DirectX12 demonstration, not evidence of a complex game lighting implementation. Separate the frame inspection window from its event list and follow how selecting an operation exposes different data. We connect a visible shape with the command that produced it.

Start with a comparison question: whether reflections retain off-screen objects, how shadow pages are updated, or which attributes a G-buffer stores. A specific question determines what to inspect among many events.

Event names guide inspection. Clearing an image and drawing a triangle have different roles. Start with the result being investigated, then select its producing operation. An item appearing in a list does not establish that it affected every pixel.

Record execution conditions: engine version, graphics API, rendering path, internal and output resolution, camera, and feature settings. Frames captured under differing conditions cannot easily isolate a single cause.

When opening a resource, inspect dimensions, format, layers, and mip levels. Determine whether it is screen-sized, light-space data, or a paged or layered structure. Names provide clues, but contents and usage relationships need verification.

First distinguish the selected event’s output. Clearing the image and drawing it have different roles in the command list. Selecting DrawInstanced reveals a colored triangle on the blue background. We now move the question from that result to mesh vertices and shader inputs.

In the recorded RenderDoc demonstration, follow the selected triangle draw and then the pixel shader’s color input and return value. This shader simply returns its input color. Locate the matching numbers as they move from input to output. This example teaches inspection, rather than demonstrating an entire lighting pipeline.

Separate position from color in the mesh and input views. Positions relate to triangle shape, while color inputs can affect appearance. A color table does not reveal every lighting quantity. First match the selected command to its shader input names.

A return value means different things at different shader stages. Do not describe a vertex-shader return as the pixel shader’s final color. Read the selected stage and input, then connect to the retained color-return demonstration. Resource names and producing operations provide more concrete evidence than appearance alone.

Now switch to our channel’s RenderDoc demonstration. Identify the selected triangle and its color input, then connect them to the shader returning that same color. Our red annotation marks the data flow being inspected. A connection verified in this simple shader does not establish the implementation of a complex lighting system in another game.

Examine a depth resource using its depth convention rather than treating it as a color image. Projected depth is generally nonlinear with physical distance. Reversed-Z can also change which numerical values represent near and far surfaces.

Match G-buffer channels to engine documentation. A normal buffer displayed as color is a visualization, not the surface's actual color. Compression and encoding must be understood before interpreting channel values as material attributes.

For shadow resources, connect the producing light with the consuming pass. Locate the transformation from a screen surface to light space and its depth comparison. Cascades and pages require examination of their partitioning and selection rules.

Switch to Unreal’s resource viewer. Several names appear, but they do not all describe the same texture. Distinguish a shadow-page pool from a virtual-texture physical pool. The earlier page discussion now connects to locating actual resources in the viewer.

After locating a name, inspect dimensions and usage. Lumen radiance data and shadow data should not be collapsed into one generic light resource. Names start the investigation; producers and consumers complete it. This viewer alone does not verify every dependency in the frame.

In reflection passes, distinguish screen-depth tracing from fallback inputs. Inspect whether probes or other trace results supply values for off-screen or occluded regions. A single reflection image does not prove that all samples were produced identically.

Volume processing may require more than viewing a color image. Separate spatial density and lighting grids from view-integrated transmittance. Grid resolution and depth partitioning connect to both artifacts and cost.

Temporal processing separates history from current inputs. Inspect which resources are written for later use and how motion and depth reject samples. A single capture may omit earlier execution conditions, so its interpretive limits need documentation.

Compare color before and after tone mapping. Locate exposure, color-space conversion, upscaling, and interface compositing in the actual passes. Do not assume an identical order in every engine or label a prepared diagram as a captured result.

Selecting an event allows its input resources to be traced back to their producers. Connecting producing and consuming commands reveals a resource's role more concretely than a feature name. Resources can also be reused for multiple purposes.

The next control concerns virtual-texture uploads. The word frame in its name does not make it frame generation. Identify the data being handled before relating the setting to the visible response. Performance-related numbers mean different things depending on which task receives the budget.

How quickly resources upload and how quickly a frame renders are different measurements. Record cache, loading and camera conditions. Having connected the resource view to its controls, the retained performance discussion now uses conditions and repeated measurements rather than one instantaneous number.

Performance requires separate measurement. Frame capture can introduce overhead or change execution behavior. Use the engine's GPU profiler and repeated runs to inspect pass timing and variability under matched conditions.
Report sample count and variation alongside averages. Check shader preparation, loading, cache state, and matched camera paths. A single frame's timing may not represent an entire scene.

Record the connections among actual resources, inputs, and outputs. Separating visual observations from implementation evidence makes the scope of each conclusion clear. This method provides a more reusable understanding than memorizing feature names.

We connected DOOM's brightness values to baked lighting, real-time shadows, screen-space effects, spatial grids, rays, caches, and final reconstruction. This was not a history in which every older technique disappeared simultaneously into one replacement.

Our first question was what gets stored. Brightness, surface attributes, depth, triangle identity, spatial lighting, and frame history contain different information. Different storage determines which questions later stages can answer.

Our second question was where the renderer searches: screen depth, a simplified spatial representation, or actual triangles. Limitations involving off-screen objects, hidden surfaces, and thin structures follow from this choice.

Our third question was how much gets computed and how results are reused. Light candidates, path samples, pages, caches, history, and reconstruction have different costs and errors. Timing changed alongside representation, sampling, hardware, and reconstruction.
When you next examine game lighting, think beyond a feature name. Understanding the data and calculations behind an image helps explain both why it looks convincing and why it breaks.
